items.title: Reactivity of the pi bond (printed as a second 11.7.1)

source_refs.note: Reactivity of the pi bond (printed as a second 11.7.1) with the Did You Know box and Quick Check 11.5, pages 257-258.

blocks.text: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes due to the presence of the double bond. The probability of finding electron is away from the line joining the two nuclei. Due to this reason π-electrons are less firmly held between the nuclei. A π bond is, therefore, a weak bond as compared to a σ-bond. During a reaction it breaks comparatively easily rendering alkenes as reactive group of compounds. Moreover, the loosely held π-electrons are more exposed to attack by the electrophilic reagents. Alkenes, therefore, undergo electrophilic addition reactions very easily.

blocks.title: Did You Know?
blocks.text: Electrophile is a species that can act as electron pair acceptor, it is represented by E⁺. Alkenes act as nucleophile because they contains pi electrons. Nucleophile is a species that can act as a donor of a pair of electrons, it is represented by Nu:⁻.

blocks.prompt: a) How does an alkane differ from an alkene in stability?
blocks.explanation: An alkane is more stable (less reactive) than an alkene. An alkane has only strong σ bonds. An alkene has a double bond whose π electrons lie away from the line joining the two nuclei and are less firmly held, so the π bond is weaker than a σ bond and breaks comparatively easily; this makes alkenes reactive.

blocks.prompt:
b) Which of the following species is likely to act as a nucleophile?
i) H₂
ii) H⁺
iii) OH⁻

blocks.explanation: OH⁻ carries a negative charge and has lone pairs of electrons that it can donate, so it acts as a nucleophile (an electron pair donor). H⁺ has no electrons to donate, and H₂ is a non-polar molecule with a filled σ bond and has neither a charge nor a lone pair.

blocks.prompt:
d) Which of the following species is likely to act as an electrophile?
i) H₂
ii) H⁺
iii) OH⁻

blocks.explanation: H⁺ has no electrons and can accept an electron pair, so it acts as an electrophile (an electron pair acceptor). OH⁻ donates electron pairs, and H₂ is a non-polar molecule with a filled σ bond and has neither a charge nor a lone pair to give or take.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Quick Check 11.5, part (c) explains the answer to (b) and part (e) the answer to (d); the printed ‘(d)’ and ‘(f)’ point to the wrong parts.

The reactions of alkenes mostly proceed through the formation of carbocations. Therefore, before studying the addition reactions of alkenes, the concept of carbocations and their stability is very important.
